title: Bob Matthews, vibes, and the planned trio
summary: Drummer and vibist Bob Matthews bridged modern and traditional jazz for him, disliked New Orleans jazz, and planned a guitar-vibes-violin trio with Bill Russell.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Fiddlers and reading violinists of New Orleans

blocks.x: I think Bob Matthews told me that Bunk used to call him. Oh, and by the way, Bob Matthews had a lot to do with my development, too, in terms of a transition between modern jazz and traditional jazz. Because, uh, I'd get together with him and we'd play vibes. He played, he was playing vibes at the time. And I'd play guitar and, uh, would play standards, you know, things written by Gershwin. And I'd begin to get used to, uh, listening, listening for that kind of thing, you know, that kind of, uh, impressionistic, harmonic thing as applied to jazz. And, uh, he was pretty important in development. And my ideas began to stretch out, too, then. And, of course, I began to listen to Segovia a lot. But, uh, basically that's, that's what, uh, happened when I was like. Who's Bob Matthews?
Uh, who's, uh, I don't know who is Bob Matthews? Yeah. He was a drummer. He's from a, Decatur, George. I can tell you about him. Very interesting, very interesting guy. Very intense.

But I couldn't figure out what he was intense about, you know. Pretty confused, I guess. I think he wanted to play the original. Like I'll do. Yeah. Bob was, I remember about Bob, he had some very valid musical ideas. We were supposed to get up a trio. You'll probably find this very interesting. I was supposed to play classic guitar. Bob was going to play vibes and Bill Russell was going to play violin. Now we were going to do this in nightclubs in New Orleans of all places, with beer drinkers, the various happy inebriates and unhappy inebriates. What did Bill Russell say about this?
